lang.thema: Gemini 4 Carbon: what it costs, who can use it, and when paying is worth it
lang.titel: GEMINI 4 CARBON PRICE: WHEN PAYING IS WORTH IT
lang.text:
I read one pricing line, and one word scared me. Gemini 4 Carbon is built to hunt software flaws, and most of us can't even use it yet. But the bug I mean isn't in code.

Here's the question this video answers. What does Carbon cost, who can use it, and when is paying actually worth it? The announcement headline calls it our next frontier model.

Be sure to like, share and save this video.

Start with the rollout paragraph. It says that starting this week, Google will make Carbon available to a subset of cyber defenders.

Cyber defenders are the people who protect systems from attackers. The same paragraph names the Fairwind Program, which will gradually phase access to additional trusted partners.

Developers, businesses and consumers come after that. The page says Google is still gathering feedback and iterating on guardrails before offering Carbon through its product surfaces as soon as possible.

The page calls this a deliberate approach, and says Google is actively engaged in the U.S. government's voluntary process for pre-release model testing.

Here's the catch. The page gives no date for wider access. Artificial Analysis, an outside tracking site, says Carbon is being rolled out to selected users and is not yet publicly available.

So why look at the price at all? Find the pricing paragraph. One word in it is the budget bug I promised.

The sentence reads: Gemini 4 Carbon will launch at the same introductory price as Argon. Argon is Google's earlier model, launched two weeks before this announcement.

The figures are $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. A token is a small chunk of text. Input is what you send. Output is what comes back.

The same sentence adds that cached input tokens are priced at 95% off the input token price.

Now look at the word introductory. Google's page doesn't say how long that price lasts. Budgets prefer the word permanent.

Artificial Analysis adds context. Its pricing bullet says $4 and $20 per million input and output tokens, with a 50% discount. It says that launch discount has no confirmed end date.

Half of $4 and $20 is $2 and $10, so the two pages line up. Still, Artificial Analysis is an outside site, so check Google's own line before you budget.

What about a free version? The announcement lists a price and a rollout plan. It never mentions a free tier for Carbon, so we won't promise one.

Free access, downloadable weights and commercial rights are three different things. The launch-price sentence promises none of them. Only token prices are written down.

So what would you be paying for? Look at the headline pitch: state-of-the-art cybersecurity performance to help build secure systems. That's where the page spends most of its numbers.

Under it come three steps: vulnerability detection, validation and remediation. A vulnerability is a software flaw an attacker could abuse. Remediation means fixing it.

The Multimodality bullet on the outside site lists text, image, video and speech input, with text output. So Carbon accepts more than text, but it writes text back.

SEC-bench Pro is the first benchmark. The page gives Carbon 88.2% for finding real vulnerabilities, and says it autonomously uncovered complex flaws buried in real-world software.

ExploitGym is second, at 54.8%. The page ties it to checking which vulnerabilities are actually exploitable, so defenders know what to remediate first.

CWE-bench, from Collinear, is third, at 71.0%. The page describes that as turning validated findings directly into working code fixes. Note the number: 71.0%, not 100%.

Now read the caption above those three scores: evaluated without guardrails. Guardrails are safety limits. These are test scores, not results on your own code.

One claim on that page goes straight at everyday coding, and it comes with a multiplier.

The page says Carbon achieves more than 2x uplift in success rate for generating secure code over Argon. Internal benchmarks means Google's own tests.

The Chrome team gets a mention too. The page says it reported Carbon performed more than 10X better than another lab's large frontier model at generating high quality patches. A patch is a code fix.

Wiz, which the page calls Google's leading cloud security platform, is quoted as well. It observes Carbon leading on benchmarks for web penetration testing, for its Scan for Good initiative.

Now the outside view. Artificial Analysis puts Carbon number 1 on its Intelligence Index v5, with 59. It holds the top score in 4 of 9 evaluations, but not in coding and knowledge work.

On its Coding Agent Index, Carbon scores 59. Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 scores 62. So for coding agents, Carbon is second.

Another bullet covers AA-Briefcase, an agentic knowledge work test. Carbon scores 1609 Elo, up 126 over Argon, but still behind Grok 4.7, Muse Wonder and Kimi K3.1 Pro.

Would cheaper per task settle it? Find the cost line. Cost per Intelligence Index task is $7.76 at standard pricing, about 23% less than Claude Opus 5.5 at $10.04.

The same bullet lists GPT-6 Astra at $6.25 per task. So cheaper than one rival isn't cheapest. Carbon uses 123k output tokens per task, versus 173k for Claude Opus 5.5.

Cheap answers only help if they're right. Open the AA-Omniscience bullet, because one number there went the wrong way.

Accuracy rises 10 points over Argon, to 58%. But the hallucination rate rises from 4% to 11%.

A hallucination is when a model states something false as fact. The page says 11% is still the second lowest of any model, behind only Argon. Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra both sit at 50%.

Back on Google's page, there's a bigger promise about long jobs. It says internally, teams have seen Carbon run for days on tasks like root-causing and patching subtle bugs across large codebases.

A job running for days invites a fear of shortcuts. Under the heading Reducing shortcuts and loophole exploitation, the page reports successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 at 0.0%, with attempts at 0.4%.

It also says high-severity misalignment alerts dropped by almost 80% in live coding environments with internal teams. Misalignment means the model behaving in ways you didn't intend. That's Google's own observation.

The safety section names a multi-layered stack: model training, real-time misuse defenses, prompt-injection resilience and chain-of-thought monitoring. Prompt injection means hidden instructions slipped into text the model reads.

Under Improved collaboration with the user in the face of ambiguity, the page says Carbon surfaces discrepancies to the user before acting. Under Greater transparency and honesty, it says unsupported claims are cut by approximately 2x over Argon.

So when would paying be worth it? The page's own focus is the clearest hint: the cybersecurity defense lifecycle, from vulnerability detection through remediation.

Hypothetically, say you maintain a small web app full of old code. Finding a flaw, checking it's real, and fixing it is the three-step job the page describes.

Hypothetically again, you only need a quick page layout. The page notes Carbon jumps +89 elo points to land at number 4, 1768, on WebDev Arena. That's a ranking, not a price tag.

Check the launch prices once more. Output costs five times input, so a job that writes a lot costs more than one that mostly reads. Cached input is priced 95% off, so repeated input costs less per token.

So here's the hidden budget bug. It's that one word, introductory. Google's page doesn't say how long the price lasts, and the outside site builds its charts on standard pricing of $4 and $20.

Right now, access starts with cyber defenders and trusted partners. For most of us, paying isn't an option yet, and the announcement lists no free tier for Carbon.

When access opens, check three lines: the token price, the cost per task and the hallucination rate. Those are the numbers on these pages that touch your wallet and your trust.

Quick recap. Carbon claims 88.2% on finding vulnerabilities, 54.8% on exploitation and 71.0% on patching, at an introductory $2 and $10. These are documented scores, not our results.

So the budget bug was never in the code. It was one word on a pricing line. Whether you can hire Carbon waits on Google's rollout. Be sure to like, share and save this video.

short.thema: ChatGPT Free vs Plus on your phone: what the pricing page lists
short.titel: ChatGPT Free: Unlimited, What The Star Hides | AI Tool #33
short.text:
ChatGPT Free says unlimited. Then comes that asterisk.

It's a tiny bouncer with a clipboard. But what's it guarding?

Fine print: unlimited text chats, subject to abuse guardrails. Be sure to like, share and save this video.

Free's input maximum: about 12 pages. Plus: 40.

Response times: Free limited, Plus Fast.

Unlimited chats, different limits elsewhere. Mind the asterisk.
